title: Shares of Global FX Reserves — the dollar, the euro and the yen
date: Data vintage: IMF COFER annual through 2025 · annual, 1980–2025
standfirst: Japan Macro Advisors' estimates of the currency composition of world foreign exchange reserves, annual from 1980. Each currency is shown as the IMF publishes it, as we extend it back, and with exchange-rate movements stripped out.
stamp: Data vintage: IMF COFER annual through 2025. The constant-rate series is valued at end-2025 exchange rates.
intro_html: The IMF publishes the currency composition of world reserves in COFER, but only from 1995. These pages carry our own series, which extends the record back to 1980, alongside the published one.
bottom_banner: The charts and data on this page are free to use and reproduce with attribution to Japan Macro Advisors. Only paid subscribers have access to this page. The series are updated once a year, when the IMF closes its COFER year.
_note: Standing dataset, not an article panel. Every value is cut from the accepted research artifacts — reserve-share-unadjusted-1975-2025-v10.csv (the observed panel), cer-v4/ (the constant-exchange-rate build) and cofer-annual-full-2026-07-27.csv (COFER as published) — never re-derived from a pipeline run. Chart form ruled by Takuji 2026-08-05: one chart per currency carrying all three measures, rather than one chart per measure carrying all three currencies. Levels and flows are published to one decimal, the precision the pre-2000 printed sources support; exhibit 6 draws only on COFER-era data and is shown to two. Rounding is half away from zero, the convention published statistics use — Python's default is half-to-even, which printed 1998 as 66.2 and made the About block's stated 0.6 gap to the Annual Report read as 0.5. A QA gate now holds that figure. The euro begins in 2000 (2001 for the flow) by Takuji's ruling of 2026-08-05: before the single currency, euro-area reserves were held in the mark, franc and guilder, and combining them involves conventions this page keeps out; the COFER line on that chart begins in 1999, its own first euro year. Deliberately absent: years before 1980, every currency outside the three, the unattributed residual as its own series, and the allocation-estimate research.

about.heading: About these statistics
about.lead: This is the methodology note from the accompanying report, reproduced here.

blocks.head: The three lines on each chart.
blocks.text: IMF COFER, as published, is the official series, which begins in 1995. JMA, Annual Reports plus COFER is our own series, carried back to 1980 and identical to the published one from 2000. At constant end-2025 rates is that same series with exchange-rate movements stripped out.

blocks.head: Where the numbers come from.
blocks.text: The IMF publishes a detailed statistic on FX reserves, Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER), with an estimate of the currency composition of the global FX reserve total. But COFER only starts in 1995, and it has a “currency unknown” part of FX reserves in 1995-1999 that the IMF only starts to allocate into currencies from 2000. Our series extends the statistics back, drawing mainly on the currency-composition tables in successive editions of the IMF's Annual Reports, supplemented by BIS statistics and national central-bank disclosures, which we used to test our reading of the “currency unknown” portion.

blocks.head: Two adjustments.
blocks.text: First, before the euro, European central banks held ECUs, claims backed by gold and US dollars. We count the dollar-backed part of the ECU as USD and drop the gold-backed part, as gold is not foreign exchange. Second, exchange rates distort shares. When the yen falls against the dollar, the yen's share in global FX reserves shrinks even if nobody sells a single yen off reserves. We therefore also compute shares with every year's holdings valued at end-2025 exchange rates, using BIS year-end rates. The ECB publishes the euro's share of global FX reserves in the same manner in its annual report, The International Role of the Euro (ECB, 2026). On this constant-exchange-rate (CER) basis, movements reflect changes in the amounts held, not in their valuation.

blocks.head: Year by year.
blocks.text: The same logic works year by year. For each year we estimate how the change in exchange rates would move the share, and read the difference from the actual change as what reserve managers added or shed. In 2022, for example, the dollar's appreciation alone would have raised its share by 1.8 points, but the share fell 0.5 points, implying managers shed about 2.2% of global FX reserves worth of USD that year. These estimates strip out exchange-rate effects only; reinvested interest income stays inside them. Our year-by-year decomposition follows the approach of Arslanalp, Eichengreen and Simpson-Bell (2022).

blocks.head: Basis.
blocks.text: All shares are shares of total global FX reserves, including the “currency unknown” portion. Full details, sources, and limitations will follow in a separate methodology report.

references_html: ECB, The International Role of the Euro, 2026.
S. Arslanalp, B. Eichengreen & C. Simpson-Bell, “The Stealth Erosion of Dollar Dominance”, IMF Working Paper 22/58, 2022.

charts.title: US dollar: three measures of its share of world reserves
charts.note: The published series begins in 1995 and is the same as ours from 2000. The shaded band spans two treatments of the portion the IMF does not attribute to a named currency.
charts._series_order: The published series is listed LAST so it draws on top. From 2000 it and the JMA series are the same numbers, and in manifest order it was hidden beneath them — which read as the official series ending in 2000. Drawn last and dotted, it tracks visibly over ours, which is the point. Do not reorder to match the legend.
